title: Two-Way Doors
explain: A two-way door is a decision you can reverse cheaply, typically anything that varies with scale: instance counts and sizes, cache TTLs, whether a module is in-process or its own service. For those I do the simplest thing that works today, and I decouple components but delay the split.
model:
Apply **minimalism** to two-way doors. The key technique:

> **Decouple the components, but delay the split.**

```
today (one deployable)              later (if scale demands)
+--------------------------+        +---------+  RPC  +---------+
| orders --iface--> billing |  -->  | orders  | ----> | billing |
|   (own tables)  (own tables)|      +---------+       +---------+
+--------------------------+
call = in-process function           call = network call; same interface
```

Keep clean boundaries in the code: modules talk through explicit interfaces and **own their own data**, yet deploy together. Splitting later is a change in *physical deployment shape*, not a rewrite of the architecture.

**The condition is real:** if modules reach into each other's tables or share global state, extraction becomes a rewrite and the door has quietly become one-way.

Extraction order: make callers use the interface only, give the module its own schema, swap the in-process call for an RPC client, then deploy separately and shift traffic gradually.

So five engineers at a few thousand requests per second need a well-structured [modular monolith](#/sd/f/scalable-simplicity), plus a careful look at the real [one-way doors](#/sd/f/one-way-door).

details.q: A team of five serves about 2,000 req/s and a teammate proposes 12 microservices with Kafka "to scale later". Your answer?
details.a: Build a modular monolith with explicit module interfaces and per-module data ownership, and extract services only when a module needs independent scaling or ownership. Process layout is a two-way door when boundaries are clean, so do not pay for distribution early.

details.q: What keeps a module cheap to extract later?
details.a: Other modules call it only through its public interface, it owns its tables with no one else querying them, and it has no hidden shared in-memory state. A separate repository is neither necessary nor sufficient.
A big ball of code where everything touches everything. It looks simple but turns the later split into a rewrite, so the two-way door becomes one-way.

details.q: Which is the most clearly a two-way door: a public ID format, an internal cache TTL, an event wire format, a webhook payload?
details.a: The internal cache TTL: a config change with a deploy and no external effect. The others are published contracts that others build on.

details.q: What changes when you extract a module into a service?
details.a: An in-process call becomes a network call: now you need timeouts, retries, partial-failure handling, serialization, and often versioned contracts. That is why you wait until scale or ownership justifies it.

details.q: How do you sequence an extraction safely?
details.a: Force all callers through the interface, give the module its own schema while still in one process, replace the call with an RPC client, then deploy separately and shift traffic gradually so you can roll back.

prompts.q: Explain "decouple the components but delay the split" and what makes it fail.
points: Clean interfaces and owned data inside one deployable
Later split changes deployment shape only
Fails when modules share tables or global state
The door then silently becomes one-way

prompts.q: Argue for a modular monolith over microservices for a small team, then say when you would split.
points: Small team and moderate load do not need distribution costs
Two-way door: reversible if boundaries are honest
Split when independent scaling, deploy cadence or ownership demands it
Mention the added failure modes of remote calls

prompts.q: Describe the steps to extract a module from a monolith into its own service.
points: Replace the in-process call with an RPC client
Deploy separately and shift traffic gradually
